title: Models of Christianity
summary: An interactive explanation of various models of Christianity — some political, others theological — and what exactly the difference between the churches is.
subtitle: Different perspectives on the diverse churches within and around the Christian religion
html:
The Three Branches Model of Christianity is the broad way that Christians refer to each other in the modern era. Nearly everyone is either Catholic (apostolic church under the leadership of the Pope), Orthodox (apostolic church with no rigid central theological authority), or Protestant (churches that broke away from Catholicism for various theological or political reasons). But this flattens the complicated relationships of the churches and how different theology can be between churches in the same branch. Pop-Catholic apologetics frequently generalizes Protestants as all having singular theology, but the differences between the denominations are sometimes vast. The Three Branches model might be somewhat useful in explaining the political history of the church, but even then it needs an update to account for Evangelicalism as a fully developed offshoot of Protestantism in its own right.

A model I think better groups churches by theology and practice is the Five Families Model. This model divides Christianity into five different families based on shared practice and theology. The differences between all churches within a group is much less drastic in this model (or a similarly sorted model).
